hint1: Everything in the world is made of these.
hint2: They are far too tiny to see, even with a school microscope.
hint3: A gold ring has billions and billions of gold ones.
hint4: 'H2O has two hydrogen ___s and one oxygen ___.'

hint1: Scientists know about 118 of these.
hint2: It can't be broken down into anything simpler.
hint3: Gold, carbon and oxygen are all examples.
hint4: Each one has a symbol, like Fe for iron or Na for sodium.

hint1: Most elements are this kind.
hint2: Pans are made of it because heat moves through it easily.
hint3: Copper, aluminium and zinc are examples.
hint4: Coins, spoons and cars are made of it.

hint1: They are on the right of the Periodic Table, except hydrogen.
hint2: Most of them do not let electricity through.
hint3: Carbon, chlorine and nitrogen are examples.
hint4: The opposite kind of element to iron and copper.

hint1: Strong ones can burn your skin, so wear goggles.
hint2: Vinegar and orange juice both have one in them.
hint3: Magnesium makes bubbles of hydrogen in it.
hint4: 'Hydrochloric ___' is in your stomach.

hint1: Chemists make many kinds, like blue copper sulfate.
hint2: Acids and metals react to make hydrogen and one of these.
hint3: 'acid + alkali → ___ + water'
hint4: The kind you put on chips is NaCl.

hint1: Elements in the same one react in a similar way.
hint2: The table of elements has eight main ones.
hint3: Lithium, sodium and potassium are all in the same one.
hint4: 'Chlorine is in ___ VII.'

hint1: The table of elements has seven of these.
hint2: Hydrogen and helium are the only two in the first one.
hint3: Lithium, carbon and neon are all in the second one.
hint4: 'Sodium is in Group I and ___ 3.'

hint1: Water, sugar and salt are all this.
hint2: Its formula has two or more different symbols, like CO2.
hint3: Its parts can only be split apart by a reaction, not by filtering.
hint4: 'Water is a ___ of hydrogen and oxygen.'

hint1: Sea water, soil and salad are all examples.
hint2: You can get each part back, for example by filtering.
hint3: Iron and sulfur powder in a jar: a magnet can still pull out the iron.
hint4: Air is one: nitrogen, oxygen and a few other gases.

hint1: Even one drop of water has billions of them.
hint2: Carbon dioxide and sugar are made of these.
hint3: Two or more tiny bits held together by bonds.
hint4: 'A water ___ is H2O.'

hint1: Sugar dissolved in water is like this.
hint2: Universal indicator turns green in it.
hint3: Neither like lemon juice nor like oven cleaner.
hint4: Pure water is this, right in the centre of the pH scale.

hint1: Shampoo bottles sometimes say theirs is 'balanced'.
hint2: It goes from 0 to 14.
hint3: Lemon juice is about 2; pure water is 7.
hint4: Universal indicator helps you find this value.

hint1: It hangs on the wall of almost every science lab.
hint2: Metals are on the left of it, non-metals on the right.
hint3: Each box in it shows a symbol, like O, Fe or Na.
hint4: A Russian scientist published the first one in 1869.

hint1: Gold is not very this, so it stays shiny for years.
hint2: Caesium, near the bottom of Group I, is extremely this.
hint3: Sodium and lithium fizz in water because they are so this.
hint4: 'Sodium is kept under oil because it is very ___.'

hint1: Every equation has at least one.
hint2: In 'magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide', there are two.
hint3: It gets used up as the change goes on.
hint4: It is written before the arrow in an equation.

hint1: In a shop it's something to buy; in chemistry it's something new.
hint2: When magnesium burns, magnesium oxide is the one formed.
hint3: Its amount grows as the reaction goes on.
hint4: It is written after the arrow in an equation.

hint1: Racing cars and baby milk use this word too.
hint2: Every compound has one, made of capitals and small digits.
hint3: It tells you which atoms are in a substance, and how many of each.
hint4: 'The ___ of water is H2O.'

hint1: It is tiny but holds almost all the mass.
hint2: A living cell has one too, in biology.
hint3: Electrons move around it in shells.
hint4: Neutrons and positive particles are packed in here.

hint1: One of three tiny pieces inside an atom.
hint2: Its mass is about the same as a neutron's.
hint3: The number of these tells you which element an atom is.
hint4: Its charge is +1, and it sits in the middle of an atom.

hint1: Almost every atom has some of these.
hint2: It has a relative mass of 1.
hint3: Carbon-12 has six of these; carbon-14 has eight.
hint4: It is neither positive nor negative.

hint1: The lightest of the three pieces in an atom.
hint2: Its relative mass is only 1/1840.
hint3: When these flow through a metal wire, we get electricity.
hint4: It has a charge of -1.

hint1: Atom diagrams show these as circles round the middle.
hint2: The first one can hold only two.
hint3: Sodium, 2,8,1, has three of these.
hint4: A snail carries one on its back.

hint1: Chemists look here to predict how an atom will react.
hint2: Atoms lose, gain or share particles from here when they bond.
hint3: For sodium, 2,8,1, it holds just one.
hint4: Noble gases don't react because theirs is full.

hint1: Table salt is made of these, not molecules.
hint2: Metals lose tiny negative particles to become these.
hint3: Each one has a plus or minus sign after its symbol.
hint4: 'Na+ is a sodium ___.'

hint1: Oven cleaner contains a strong one.
hint2: It feels soapy and has a pH above 7.
hint3: Ammonia solution and limewater are examples.
hint4: It dissolves in water to give OH- ions, like NaOH.

hint1: Indigestion tablets contain one to settle your stomach.
hint2: Every metal hydroxide is one.
hint3: It reacts with H+ ions to make a salt and water.
hint4: An alkali is the kind that dissolves in water.

hint1: Farmers spread lime on fields to make this happen.
hint2: Taking an indigestion tablet starts this reaction in your stomach.
hint3: NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H2O is an example.
hint4: In this reaction, the pH moves towards 7.

hint1: A few drops of it tell you about a solution.
hint2: Red cabbage juice works as a natural one.
hint3: In a titration, it shows you when to stop.
hint4: Litmus and methyl orange are two of these.

hint1: Marble statues and eggshells are mostly made of one.
hint2: Acids react with it to make a salt, water and CO2.
hint3: Its ion is CO3 with a 2- charge.
hint4: 'Sodium ___ is washing soda.'

hint1: Drain cleaner often contains one.
hint2: Its ion has one oxygen and one hydrogen, with a negative charge.
hint3: Copper ions make a pale blue one in lab tests.
hint4: 'Limewater is calcium ___ solution.'

hint1: They are kept under oil in the school lab.
hint2: You can cut them with a knife.
hint3: They fizz in water, giving off hydrogen.
hint4: Lithium, rubidium and caesium are three of these.

hint1: Their name comes from Greek words meaning 'salt maker'.
hint2: They are coloured, poisonous non-metals.
hint3: Each atom has seven electrons in its outer shell.
hint4: Fluorine is the most reactive one of all.

hint1: They almost never form compounds.
hint2: They sit in the far right column of the Periodic Table.
hint3: Party balloons are filled with the lightest one.
hint4: Argon, krypton and xenon are three of them.

hint1: You describe one when you look at data in a table or graph.
hint2: Words like 'rises', 'falls' and 'gets bigger' describe one.
hint3: Going down Group I, metals get more reactive: that's one.
hint4: 'The ___ is that melting points get lower down Group I.'

hint1: Plastic and wood are bad at doing this.
hint2: Copper is used in wires because it does this so well.
hint3: Melted salt can do it, but solid salt cannot.
hint4: To let a current or warmth pass through.

hint1: Teachers often ask for this before the harder version with formulae.
hint2: It has plus signs and an arrow, but no formulae.
hint3: Each substance is written out in full, like 'sodium chloride'.
hint4: 'magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide' is one.

hint1: A healthy diet should be this.
hint2: You may need big numbers in front of formulae to make it this.
hint3: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O is this; H2 + O2 → H2O is not.
hint4: Like weighing scales that are perfectly level.

hint1: Each box in the Periodic Table shows it.
hint2: The Periodic Table is arranged by this, going up from 1.
hint3: For carbon it is 6, for oxygen 8.
hint4: It counts the positive particles in the centre.

hint1: It is written at the top left of a chemical symbol.
hint2: Isotopes of one element have different values of it.
hint3: In carbon-14, the 14 is this.
hint4: It counts all the heavy particles in the middle of an atom.

hint1: The Periodic Table position of an element lets you work it out.
hint2: Its last figure usually matches the group number.
hint3: For chlorine it is 2,8,7.
hint4: How the negative particles are spread over the energy levels, e.g. 2,8,1.

hint1: Some kinds are radioactive and used in medicine.
hint2: They have the same chemical properties but different masses.
hint3: Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 are two of these.
hint4: Same atomic number, different mass number.

hint1: Every salt contains this kind of particle.
hint2: In electrolysis, it is pulled to the negative electrode.
hint3: Na+, Mg2+ and Al3+ are examples.
hint4: Any charged particle with a plus sign.

hint1: In electrolysis, it is pulled towards the positive electrode.
hint2: Chloride, oxide and sulfate are all this kind.
hint3: Its name often ends in '-ide', like bromide.
hint4: A charged particle with a minus sign, like Cl-.

hint1: It holds magnesium oxide together.
hint2: It forms between a metal and a non-metal.
hint3: Sodium gives an electron to chlorine, and then this holds them.
hint4: Not covalent: the kind that holds NaCl together.

hint1: It holds the atoms together inside a water molecule.
hint2: It forms between two non-metal atoms.
hint3: Shown as a dot and a cross where two circles overlap.
hint4: H2 has one; O2 has a double one.

hint1: Exam questions on bonding often ask for one.
hint2: Overlapping circles in it show shared pairs.
hint3: It uses two marks so you can tell which atom each particle came from.
hint4: 'Show the bonding in HCl with a ___.'

hint1: Volcanoes pour out rock in this state.
hint2: Steelworks pour iron in this state into moulds.
hint3: Candle wax near the flame is in this state.
hint4: Ionic compounds conduct when dissolved or ___.

hint1: Many reactions in test tubes use chemicals in this form.
hint2: It shares a Latin root with 'aquarium'.
hint3: Its state symbol is two letters in brackets.
hint4: The sugar in a cup of sweet tea is this.

hint1: Chemists anywhere can read it, whatever language they speak.
hint2: It uses H2O instead of the name 'water'.
hint3: You can add (s), (l), (g) or (aq) to each part.
hint4: '2Mg + O2 → 2MgO' is one.

hint1: It goes after each formula in a full equation.
hint2: It shows the physical form of each substance.
hint3: (aq) is the one for something dissolved in water.
hint4: In '2Mg(s) + O2(g)', the (s) and (g) are these.

hint1: Glucose's is C6H12O6.
hint2: It can be a whole-number multiple of the simplest ratio.
hint3: For ethene it is C2H4, not CH2.
hint4: It gives the true count of each element in one particle, like CH4.

hint1: It comes from lichens, small plant-like living things.
hint2: It comes as a purple solution or on thin strips.
hint3: A '___ test' also means a question that shows what someone really believes.
hint4: It tells you acid or alkali, but not the exact pH.

hint1: It is a blend of several dyes.
hint2: Unlike litmus, it shows how strongly acidic or alkaline something is.
hint3: Green means neutral; purple means a strong alkali.
hint4: Match its shade to a chart to get a value from 0 to 14.

hint1: They often act as catalysts.
hint2: Their compounds are often brightly coloured.
hint3: They sit in the wide central block of the Periodic Table.
hint4: Nickel, chromium and cobalt are examples.

hint1: All the halogens are like this.
hint2: Hydrogen, nitrogen and oxygen gases are all like this.
hint3: Each particle is like identical twins, bonded together.
hint4: Chlorine gas is Cl-Cl, not single Cl, because it is this.

hint1: It has no units, though it tells you how heavy something is.
hint2: You can read it for every element from the Periodic Table.
hint3: Its symbol is Ar.
hint4: 'The ___ of chlorine is 35.5.'

hint1: You need it to turn grams into moles.
hint2: Its symbol is Mr.
hint3: For CO2 it is 44: 12 + 16 + 16.
hint4: 'The ___ of water is 18.'

hint1: It keeps a balloon stuck to a wall after you rub it on your hair.
hint2: It explains why NaCl has such a high melting point.
hint3: In an ionic bond, it holds the + and - particles together.
hint4: Plus and minus come together, like north and south on magnets.

hint1: Neon, argon and krypton exist like this.
hint2: Its gas particles are not joined to any partner.
hint3: Its formula is only a symbol with no small number after it.
hint4: 'Unlike chlorine, Cl2, argon is ___.'

hint1: Drop a vitamin C tablet in water to see it.
hint2: Cola and champagne show lots of it when you open them.
hint3: It shows that a reaction is giving off CO2 or hydrogen.
hint4: 'When magnesium was added to the acid, there was ___.'

hint1: Garden fences and pie tops can have this criss-cross pattern too.
hint2: Diamond and graphite are giant covalent ones.
hint3: Sodium chloride forms a giant ionic one.
hint4: 'Metals have a ___ of positive ions in a sea of electrons.'

hint1: Graphite has them between its layers, so it conducts.
hint2: They are why copper conducts heat and electricity so well.
hint3: They are not held by any one atom.
hint4: Negative particles that roam through the whole lattice.

hint1: Chemists can work it out from masses measured in an experiment.
hint2: For ionic compounds like NaCl, this is the only kind used.
hint3: Glucose is C6H12O6, but this is CH2O.
hint4: Cancel C2H4 down as far as it goes and you get this: CH2.

hint1: Chemists use it to count things far too tiny to count one by one.
hint2: The mass of one, in grams, equals the relative formula mass.
hint3: It contains 6.02 × 10²³ of whatever you are counting.
hint4: It shares its name with a small animal that digs tunnels.

hint1: It is not the same as 'concentrated', though people often confuse them.
hint2: At equal concentration, it has a lower pH than ethanoic.
hint3: Every one of its molecules splits into ions in water.
hint4: Sulfuric, nitric and the one in your stomach are examples.

hint1: It is not the same as 'dilute', though students often mix the two up.
hint2: At equal concentration, its pH is higher than hydrochloric's.
hint3: Only a few of its molecules split into ions in water.
hint4: Citric, in lemons, and carbonic, in cola, are examples.

hint1: The Brønsted-Lowry theory uses this phrase.
hint2: A more scientific way to describe anything with a pH below 7.
hint3: HCl is one: it passes its H+ to water.
hint4: Any substance that hands over H+ ions in a reaction.

hint1: Acids and soluble salts do this in water.
hint2: Strong acids do it fully; weak ones only partly.
hint3: HCl does it in water, giving H+ and Cl-.
hint4: To come apart into charged particles.
